key_insight: A finite-chord compressible scattering model predicts leading-edge noise reduction for perforated and porous inserts without fitted acoustic constants by deriving the insert admittance from measurable geometry and flow physics.
engineering_relevance: This enables more reliable design of low-noise airfoil leading edges for turbomachinery and aeroacoustics, with better transfer from test data to real hardware.
method: Solved the finite-chord, compressible subsonic leading-edge scattering problem with arbitrary chordwise admittance, including wake shedding, Kutta condition, and permeability-dependent edge singularities.
Derived perforated-insert admittance from Rayleigh conductivity with corrections for plate thickness, aperture interaction, and grazing-flow blockage.
Modeled bulk porous inserts using measured permeability and pore-fluid inertia, then closed the far field with finite-span and array-aperture effects.
evidence_signal: For three perforated inserts across four flow conditions, the model matched measurements to 2.5 dB rms over 84 comparisons versus 4.4 dB for the earlier scaled-impedance approach; two of three porous inserts were predicted within 1.7 dB rms.
watch_item: A narrow tonal peak pattern seen on perforated plates was not captured by the tested admittances, suggesting an additional convecting source mechanism beyond the frozen-gust assumption.
paper_title: Leading-edge noise reduction by perforated and porous inserts: a compressible finite-chord prediction without fitted constants
